author: blu
body: max-parse-stall bounds the thing that actually goes wrong: consecutive fuel-consuming calls at the SAME token position. A parse that progresses resets it, so no legitimate program can reach it however deeply nested -- the grammar chain at any one token is tens of calls, not thousands. A parse that cannot progress reaches it in microseconds and says so.

author: blu
body: max-list-literal-elems is an EMITTER limit that the type checker enforces on the checker's behalf, because the emitter cannot report it.

author: blu
body: The bound is therefore no longer the binding constraint and is kept unchanged for now on purpose: raising it is a separate change that has to establish what the NEXT limit is and pin it with a test, rather than inherit a number sized for a cost that no longer exists.

author: blu
body: That guard had a hole of its own for a day, and it is the instructive kind: it fired correctly and then the WIND-DOWN overran the ceiling. __linked-list-to-list runs inside deck-record, so converting the collected tokens wrote eight bytes per token onto the deck that had just overflowed, against a flat one-megabyte band. `-Decks 5` fires early enough to fit; `-Decks 20` fired late and converted straight through the ceiling into the bivy. The overflow path now discards the tokens, which costs nothing because compile-lex already returns `tokens = []` once the bag has errors.

author: blu
body: demand-desugar-floor was raised from 64 MB to 72 MB in the same change, by exactly the band width, so the guard costs no USABLE floor. Address space is the only cost of a floor, which is what makes paying for the band this way free.

author: blu
body: On saturation desugar-document returns an EMPTY chapter rather than the truncated one, which is the LEX lesson applied rather than learned twice: a wind-down that allocates in proportion to what it collected walks through the ceiling it just refused to cross.

author: blu
body: The rule stands as PhaseAllocator states it: the predicate follows the EXTENT the loop sits in, and neither reading is safe to assume from the phase's name.

author: blu
body: There was never an INLINE phase. demand-inline-floor sat here as a dead constant, read by nothing, and its presence alone was enough to put a third phase into the deck-guard work that no reservation and no deck ever corresponded to. The inline passes run inside run-ir-pipeline, on the LOWER deck. The constant is deleted.

author: blu
body: The quotation gate runs before the frontend does, and it parses the source to find the quotations it must gate. That parse needs decks of its own, because the frontend has not raised any yet. The scratch floor carries the tokens and the syntax tree of a parse that is thrown away, so it is sized as a LEX and a PARSE together; the keep floor carries the one thing that survives, the text of the works we admitted, so it is sized as source text and is checked against before it is written.
